summary: Offers shared vocabulary for talking about directory systems, giving definitions so that people discussing them can agree on terms. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before arguing about phone books, everyone agrees what words like entry and lookup mean. This is that list of words.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary for describing information access systems

tldr.problem: When discussing directory and information access systems like DNS and LDAP, engineers used the same terms but meant different things, making standardization work unclear.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3254 defines shared terminology along six dimensions: uniqueness and scope (global vs local, centralized vs distributed), access methods (lookup vs search), consistency models (strict to loose), security models (trust and access control), update policies (read-only to write-mostly), and the specific meaning of 'directory' (search capability plus convergent consistency).
tldr.outcome: The shared vocabulary lets engineers specify what kind of repository they are building and compare existing systems like DNS, X.500, BGP and LDAP using consistent language.

facts.label: Consistency types
facts.value: Strict, internal, converging, loose, or none

today: RFC 3254 remains the standard vocabulary for discussing directory and information systems in Internet standards. The six-dimensional framework it defines is still used to classify new protocols and systems, and the examples it gives of real systems (DNS, LDAP, BGP, SNMP) are still accurate.

sections.title: Why Shared Terminology Matters
sections.content: The Internet contains many systems for making information accessible: the Domain Name System, LDAP directories, routing databases, telephone directories, and file systems. When engineers discuss building new information access systems, they often use the same terms to mean different things. For example, one person might call something a 'directory' and another might call it a 'repository', and they might be describing different properties. RFC 3254 defines a shared vocabulary with clear boundaries so that an Internet standards document can precisely specify what kind of information system it describes. The vocabulary covers six main dimensions: scope (global vs local), distribution (centralized vs distributed), access methods, consistency, security, and update patterns. Using these definitions, different systems can be compared and understood clearly.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems let you search, others only let you look up an exact entry. Some might have old or new information at different locations. These words mean specific things so engineers can talk clearly.

sections.title: Six Dimensions of Repository Design
sections.content: RFC 3254 defines repository characteristics along six independent dimensions. Scope and uniqueness: A global repository can exist only once in the world (like E.164 telephone numbering); a local repository can have independent copies. A centralized repository passes all access through one site; a distributed repository can access through multiple sites. A replicated repository has all information at all sites; a cooperative repository distributes information but can route requests to find it. Access methods: A lookup requires knowing an exact value and returns one result (binary yes/no); a search takes approximate input and returns zero, one or many matches. A query repository answers once and stops; a notify or subscription repository sends updates when data changes. Consistency: Strict consistency means all sites always match; strict internal consistency means replies are logically consistent but might be from different versions; loose converging consistency means sites will eventually match if updates stop; inconsistency means no guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: Information systems vary in how many copies exist, whether you must know exactly what you're looking for, how fresh the information is, and who can change it.

sections.title: Security and Update Models
sections.content: Security models address two things: why you trust data, and how you get access. On trust: perimeter integrity assumes data is correct because it is in an authorized repository; item integrity uses digital signatures; hopeful integrity assumes data is correct because it makes sense with other information. On access: open access lets anyone in; property-based access checks what or where you are; identity-based access checks who you are (username/password or certificates); token-based access checks what you have (a shared password or certificate). Update models range from read-only (no standard update method) to read-mostly (few updates, slow consistency) to read-write (equal reads and writes) to write-mostly (high volume of updates, with reproduction on demand). These are independent dimensions: DNS is global lookup but can be read-only or read-mostly with DynDNS; BGP is global read-write; SNMP agents are local read-write.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems let anyone view information, others require passwords. Some are hard to change, others are constantly updated. The trust might come from a trusted gatekeeper or from signatures on the information itself.

sections.title: What Makes a 'Directory'
sections.content: Throughout the RFC, the term 'directory' is used carefully. In the most common usage, a system is worthy of being called a directory only if it has two properties: search capability (not just lookup) and convergent consistency (not just any consistency model). Otherwise the six dimensions can vary. The DNS is a global cooperative lookup repository with loose converging consistency and query-only capability. X.500 was intended as a global search repository with loose converging consistency. LDAP directories are typically local, centralized, with search and lookup, and read-mostly. A BGP routing table is a global read-write repository with loose non-converging subset consistency. These distinctions matter: you cannot search the DNS for 'all entries containing smith' the way you search an LDAP directory; DNS is lookup-only. Conversely, BGP is not a directory by this definition because its consistency does not converge.
sections.plainLanguage: A 'directory' is a system where you can search and find complete information when you check again later. Some systems store information one way, others another way, but directories have these two key features.

sections.title: Using the Vocabulary
sections.content: When designing or describing an information system, an RFC can now say things like: 'This protocol defines a local, centralized, read-mostly repository with lookup capability, strict internal consistency, and open access.' That statement conveys six independent design choices. The RFC classifies several real systems: DNS (global, cooperative, lookup, loose converging consistency, read-only or read-mostly, open access, perimeter integrity); X.500 (global search, loose converging, read-mostly, perimeter, query); BGP (global read-write, loose non-converging subset consistency, access by what you are); NetNews (global read-write, non-converging subset, both search and lookup, subscription); SNMP agents (local, centralized, lookup, read-write, access by what you have). Using this shared vocabulary in standards documents prevents ambiguity and helps engineers make deliberate choices rather than inheriting unclear assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: When the next engineer designs a system, they can use these words to say exactly what it does—is it just for looking up, or searching? Will it always have the latest information, or might it be old? Who can see it?
